paragraphs.source_en: Half-moon like object attached on one or both shoulders may be one of the oldest and most important attributes because it is present already with the Kel Essuf engravings in the Algerian Tadrart. The Kel Essuf are anthropomorphic figures of extremely simple forms and the care taken to represent the half-moon objects or horns on almost shapeless bodies indicates the importance which they had in that society. These objects may have been visible signs indicating a certain social degree. If these were so important that they were the only attributes represented, they may have been worn by certain individuals only. In this sense the engraved figures possibly represented a certain social group, such as the initiated men. Halfmoon objects in the Kel Essuf art may therefore indicate what kind of individual was represented and what his or her status was in the society.

paragraphs.source_en: The bracelet is another attribute appearing on Round Head figures in the Tassili Plateau (Fig. 5-21). Except for one female figure at Sefar, this object is exclusively associated to men. Its position on the body is probably significant because in 90% of cases the bracelets are depicted on the left hand. The prevalent placement on the left side may not have been a simple habit or fashion but it may have had a deep meaning. The ritual and spiritual distinction of the left and right side is very marked in virtually all African societies, where each side is assigned different qualities. The Songhay in Niger believe that evil spirits enter the human body through the left middle finger, and that is why they wear big rings on this finger to protect themselves against the harmful power (Stoller & Olkes 1987).

paragraphs.source_en: The fact that the attributes are associated almost exclusively to male figures is rather significant. Supposing that the various attributes were indicators of the individual's status in the society, it must be stated that they would have expressed a different social status between males in a group and also a different social status between men and women. The only phenomenon attributed to both men and women is the body decoration of various motifs. Dots and lines in the paintings may also represent scarifications or tattoos, still used in the Sahara and in the Sub-Saharan Africa today.
